keyframe_review.note: New keyframe 900-1599: the page places the Tairona in the Sierra Nevada de Santa Marta 'across present-day Cesar, Magdalena, and La Guajira in Colombia' and gives no area. A 90 km disc round Santa Marta (about 11,900 km2 of land) stands for the massif and its coast (my reading).

ledger.note: c. 900: the Tairona period begins. A 'hierarchical network of villages that developed around 900' and the 'Tairona period begins from c. 900 CE'; the tradition's 'definitive formation as an independent cultural tradition goes back to at least the 10th and 11th centuries AD'. The page calls them 'a group of different chiefdoms'.

region.text: the site of Santa Marta on the Caribbean coast

ledger.note: 29 July 1525: the Spanish found Santa Marta. 'Founded on July 29, 1525, by the Spanish conqueror Rodrigo de Bastidas'; the Santa Marta page does not say the site was Tairona land or that anyone was displaced.

region.text: the Sierra Nevada de Santa Marta and its coast, across present-day Cesar, Magdalena and La Guajira

ledger.note: 1600: the Tairona revolt and the end of the chiefdoms' independence, as the page implies. The page gives no end date for independence; its only dated conflict is 'the 1600 revolt', after which 'a class of priests later took power', and says confrontations with the Spanish grew by 1600; the cited source's title covers Spanish-indigenous conflict from 1501 to 1600. The year is the page's only date; the land passing to Spain is the reading.

certainty.note: A massif of chiefdoms with no borders on the page.

notes: Typed 'culture': 'a group of different chiefdoms' with 'a hierarchical network of villages'; no capital is named (Ciudad Perdida is only an archaeological project on the page), so identity.capitals is empty. The page gives no end of independence: 1600 is the only dated event, so the dissolve is confidence 1. Santa Marta's 1525 founding is the only Spanish date on the pages read; Spanish expeditions into the Sierra are not on either page. A source cited by the page covers the Spanish-Indigenous conflict 1501-1600; the page's ceramic chronology runs to 1650. The Santa Marta page is a city article with one dated sentence.
